Unemployment Insurance Act class of people does not wish to take the responsibility of being independent or private enterprise operators of farms but still wishes to continue in that way of life, I feel that there should be some basic security presented by proper legislation to see to it that in times of seasonal unemployment they will be protected. I feel sure that the Gill royal commission will come up with the answer to this problem. I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that personally-and I think I am speaking on behalf of my constituents of Moose Mountain-I feel that they are definitely in favour of the motion brought in by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING BENEFITS FOR SEASONAL FARM LABOURERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on this particular motion which was introduced by my colleague and neighbour the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale. I was rather amused when the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the way in which rotation was taking place in the Liberal party in the matter of agricultural spokesmen. It rather reminded me of the description of a hula dancer: put a crop here and put a crop there and then you rotate the crops. Perhaps this is typical of the Liberal party. They have been used to passing the buck and perhaps they do not wish to take the responsibility for being spokesmen. However, other members have expressed reasons why this type of legislation should be introduced and why the government should make a careful study of it.
It has been mentioned that competent help has been hard to get. Often times we have been obliged to resort to very young labourers, some of them just fresh out of school, who have not been able to establish themselves. Many of these young people have a farm background. They know the farm way of life and would far rather have it than perhaps any other. However, because of insecurity in that type of employment they often drift off the farms into other employment which would provide them with some security in the event they were laid off. I know that in my own particular case I myself have been obliged to employ many of these people. Sometimes you get an experienced hand. You often find that where a man has been laid off because of some farmer having quit farming and no longer requiring him, he has to make a shift but in making that shift very often finds himself in a position in which he is obliged to resort to using the money he has been able to save over the years, if he is lucky enough to have any. However, this creates a particular problem.


I know that on many occasions, especially during the rush season, in the spring and fall, for example, many young girls have been employed in the fields driving tractors, combines, trucks and so on. Many women and older labourers have taken to the fields at times like this. I think this situation could be corrected if legislation like this could possibly be enacted.
It was mentioned by the hon. member for Rosthern that many farmers have been obliged to purchase expensive machinery as a result of the fact that they could not get help. For one thing they would then require less help. Another point is that the type of machinery they have purchased is very expensive. I can give many examples of what happened in my own case-but that is unnecessary-where you turn over expensive machinery to young, inexperienced help. Another problem that par-haps could be corrected if this type of legislation were enacted is this. The fact is that many farmers have had to pay higher wages as a result of many people no longer wishing to stay with or work on farms because of the insecurity in that field.
I should like to raise another point which I believe was mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Contractors working on the clearing of farmland find that when they hire a machine operator to clear the bush or to do brushing in preparation for cultivation, that man is not insurable. However, if the same contractor is doing work for the municipality, he is insurable. He may have two machines operating side by side, one on the farmer's property and the other on the road allowance. The man operating the machine on the road allowance is insurable and the man working on the farm is not although they are operating identical machines. They are doing the same type of work and are working just as hard but one man is insurable and the other man is not. This problem would be corrected by the introduction of such legislation.
There are cases one could cite. For instance, men who work on irrigation projects are insurable but others, as I said, are not. This is a problem that needs a little study in order to correct some of these inequities.
Having said that, I think I should point out some of the difficulties that exist in implementing legislation of this type. There are very few countries that have similar legislation in existence so we cannot make a study of their plans in order to incorporate them into ours.
I think Great Britain was the first country to set up such a plan away back in 1911. However, even after having had such a plan in operation for some 35 years I understand

that in one year there were some 30,000 inquiries as to how it could be made operative and applicable in certain cases. Although they have had 35 years experience they still have not been able to solve the problem.
I might also say that because of the scattered nature of farming one would run into difficulty. In many cases it would be difficult to ascertain whether or not a man was actually employed. I am merely pointing out these things to illustrate some of the difficulties that would be encountered if such legislation were introduced. Only if some of these problems can be ironed out will we be able to arrive at proper legislation.
Another point has to do with whether the employee is a member of the family. It is often difficult to determine what rate of pay a man receives if he is a member of the family. What kind of stamp would you provide for him? There are cases where room and board are provided and others where board alone is provided and the man provides his own room. There are other cases where the man receives only his wages with no room or board provided.
These are some of the things that have to be considered before a suitable arrangement can be worked out. I simply wish to mention these things and to point out that the matter is now under study. I hope that before long the Gill commission will be able to make some suitable recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to have considerably more time than I apparently will have in order to develop my speech on the resolution brought forward by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp).
I must say at once that when the hon. member introduces a private member's bill or resolution in the house one must pay very strict attention indeed because his record of success with regard to the proposals he has placed before parliament is practically unique. It is a great credit to him and to the government which has encouraged the active participation of the private members who support the government, unlike the days not too long ago when the trained seals flapped their flippers and kept solemnly quiet. A lot of people thought that things would be interesting after these trained seals were unleashed, but lo and behold, we find that not many of them have had anything to say in the interval.

I want to deal very quickly with the resolute, positive, forward looking alternative that the Liberal party is supplying according to this document referred to by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) where I find these words:
The Liberal party has, for today's problems, the answers that are progressive, realistic and responsible.
One might have expected upon examining this document to find a clear, concise and aggressive statement of a practical, alternative policy. But what do we find? Nothing on this particular question. Let hon. members listen carefully to these words:
Unemployment insurance should be extended to as many farm workers as possible.
Not "unemployment insurance will be extended". Oh, no; "should be extended". To how many or to what group of people? As many as possible.
